script.opening: “Hi, it’s Jordan Fletcher. The nurse said to ring for my blood results. I just want to know what they are — I’m not going into hospital, so please don’t ask me.”

facts.text: “Knackered. Out of breath on the stairs. Heart racing. Light-headed when I stand up quick.” No collapse, no chest pain.

facts.topic: Stools (if asked about bowels or bleeding)
facts.text: “They’ve been black, like tar, every day for about five days. Smell horrible.” No fresh red blood. Not taking iron or Pepto-Bismol.
No vomiting, no blood or coffee grounds. “Burning in the top of my stomach, goes through to my back sometimes. Worse after a drink.” No difficulty swallowing. Appetite poor; jeans a bit looser.
“I stopped the omeprazole ages ago — felt fine. I didn’t finish the antibiotics either.” Takes ibuprofen “now and then” for his back — three or four this week.

“Eight cans a day — normal lager, the big cans.” First drink “when I get up, to stop the shakes.” Has had sweats and shakes when he has tried to stop before; no fits. Feels guilty about it. Started after the split with Mia’s mum a year ago.

“Last time they treated me like a drunk. Left me on a trolley all night.” If asked more, or if the doctor seems kind: “And I’ve got my daughter this week. Mia’s seven. Her mum’s in Spain till Sunday. There’s no-one.”

facts.topic: Deeper fear (only if the doctor asks what worries him about Mia or social services)
facts.text: “If I end up in hospital with my drinking, her mum will find out and that’s it — I won’t see her. Or social services get involved.”

Sister Leanne lives 15 minutes away; “she’d have Mia, probably, but I haven’t asked — she’s sick of me.” Does not drive at the moment. Unemployed since redundancy, on Universal Credit. Smokes 10 a day. No drugs.

Can repeat back accurately what the doctor said about bleeding and the risk of collapse or death, and weighs it: “I get it — I could die. But I’m not leaving Mia tonight.” Not drunk now — had two cans this morning.

Be defensive at first, softening if the doctor is non-judgemental. Refuse admission tonight whatever is said. If the doctor offers a concrete plan for Mia (asking Leanne) and does not threaten social services, agree to: Leanne staying tonight, a call from the hospital team, and going to the hospital assessment unit tomorrow morning if they can see him. Agree to call 999 if you vomit blood or collapse.

ice.ideas: “I’m anaemic because I don’t eat properly.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he is the only adult caring for his 7-year-old daughter this week and fears that admission will expose his drinking and cost him contact with her; he also felt judged on a ward last time.
ice.expectations: Results, maybe some iron tablets, and to stay at home.

cues: “I’m not going into hospital, so don’t ask.” — a reason is waiting to be explored.
“Last time they treated me like a drunk.” — shame and a bad experience.
“There’s no-one.” — a child who depends on him tonight.

checkpoints.text: Interprets the results in context: Hb 74 microcytic, raised urea with normal creatinine, tachycardia and low BP — and asks about melaena, haematemesis, epigastric pain, NSAIDs and the incomplete H. pylori treatment
Takes an alcohol history that identifies dependence (morning drinking, withdrawal symptoms) and recognises a high-risk upper GI bleed needing same-day hospital assessment
Explores the reasons for refusal and finds the daughter at home and the fear of losing contact
Clearly recommends same-day hospital assessment and explains the risks of refusing (further bleeding, collapse, death); assesses and documents capacity for this decision

Negotiates the safest alternative: an adult for Mia tonight, discussion with the on-call medical or gastroenterology team today (earliest ambulatory assessment and endoscopy), PPI as agreed, thiamine, stop NSAIDs, no iron yet
Advises against stopping alcohol suddenly, offers alcohol service support, gives explicit 999 triggers (vomiting blood, collapse, more black stool, chest pain) and arranges a same-day call-back
Non-judgemental throughout; addresses the child’s safety honestly without threat; respects his autonomy while keeping the offer of admission open

worked.txt: “Your blood count is about half what it should be, and another test suggests blood is being digested in the gut. With the black stools and your old ulcer, I think the ulcer is bleeding again.”
“You said straight away you wouldn’t go into hospital. Can you tell me what’s behind that?”
“I have to be straight with you: a bleeding ulcer can suddenly get much worse. People can collapse, and some die. That’s why I’m recommending hospital today.”
“Just so I know I’ve explained it properly — can you tell me in your own words what might happen if you stay at home?”
“This isn’t about getting anyone involved — it’s that if you collapse tonight, Mia would be alone with you. Could Leanne come over or have her?”

f.learning: A refusal is the start of the conversation, not the end. Explore the reason (here: a child at home, fear of losing contact, previous stigma), give honest information about risk including death, then assess capacity for the specific decision (understand, retain, use or weigh, communicate — Mental Capacity Act 2005). An unwise decision does not mean incapacity, and recent alcohol does not automatically remove capacity. If he has capacity, respect the refusal (GMC decision-making and consent guidance) and reduce risk: speak to the on-call medical or gastroenterology team today (many units offer next-day ambulatory endoscopy for patients who decline admission), agree PPI with them, stop NSAIDs, prescribe thiamine for a dependent drinker, advise against abrupt alcohol cessation, avoid starting oral iron before endoscopy (it blackens stools and confuses monitoring), give clear 999 advice, and document thoroughly. When a dependent child is at home with a parent at risk of collapse, secure another adult now. H. pylori status should be rechecked (at endoscopy, or by stool antigen or breath test at least two weeks off PPI).

knowledge.summary: High-risk upper GI bleed in a dependent drinker who declines admission: find the reason, give honest risk, assess capacity, protect the child, and negotiate the safest next step with the on-call team.

points.h: Recognising a significant upper GI bleed
points.t: Melaena, haematemesis or coffee-ground vomit; tachycardia, low BP, postural symptoms; Hb drop; urea raised out of proportion to creatinine. The Glasgow-Blatchford score uses urea, Hb, systolic BP, pulse, melaena, syncope, hepatic disease and heart failure — a score of 0 is low risk; here it is around 14.

Decision-specific and time-specific. Presume capacity; take practicable steps to help him decide. Test: understand, retain, use or weigh, communicate. Document the information given, his reasoning and the outcome. Intoxication can impair capacity — check whether he is intoxicated now.

Respect the decision, keep the offer open, and negotiate the next best option: on-call team advice, earliest ambulatory endoscopy, clear return triggers, someone with him, a call-back. Never imply he cannot come back later.

Stop NSAIDs. A PPI (for example omeprazole — usual adult dose 20–40 mg once daily; NICE/SPC; check the SPC and local formulary; SPC: omeprazole) as agreed with the on-call team. Thiamine for dependent drinkers (usual adult dose 100 mg two or three times daily orally; NICE/SPC; check the SPC and local formulary; SPC: thiamine). Defer oral iron until the bleeding source is assessed.

Morning drinking and withdrawal symptoms mean dependence: do not advise stopping suddenly (withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens). Offer referral to the community alcohol service for assisted withdrawal; AUDIT and SADQ help quantify. Raised GGT and ALT fit alcohol; check liver status later.
Incomplete eradication and no test of cure: test at endoscopy, or by stool antigen or urea breath test at least 2 weeks after stopping PPI and 4 weeks after antibiotics.

A seven-year-old alone with a parent at risk of collapse is a safety issue now. Secure another responsible adult tonight. Consider whether wider safeguarding advice is needed, and be open with him about that rather than threatening.

model.text: Hello Jordan, it’s Dr Hussain. Thanks for ringing. Before the results — how have you been since you saw the nurse?
Knackered, out of breath. Just tell me the results — and I’m not going into hospital.
OK, I’ll be straight with you. Your blood count is quite low. Can I ask a few questions to work out why? Have your stools been black, or have you vomited any blood?
Black every day for five days. No sick. Burning in my stomach.
Any ibuprofen or aspirin? Did you finish the ulcer treatment last time? And how much are you drinking at the moment — do you need a drink in the morning?
A few ibuprofen. Didn’t finish the tablets. Eight cans a day; first thing, yeah, for the shakes.

Thank you for being honest. I think your ulcer is bleeding again. Your blood count is half what it should be, your heart is racing to make up for it, and a bleed like this can suddenly get worse — people can collapse and some die. I’m recommending you go to hospital today for a camera test and treatment.
No. Last time they treated me like a drunk.
That sounds like it was horrible, and I’m sorry. Is there anything else making today difficult?
I’ve got Mia, my daughter, this week. Her mum’s away. If I end up in hospital with the drinking, I’ll lose her.
You’re trying to protect her — that matters. Can you tell me in your own words what could happen if you stay at home?
It could bleed more, I could pass out, I could die. I get it. I’m still not leaving her tonight.

I respect that it’s your decision. But if you collapse tonight, Mia would be alone with you. Could your sister stay over or have her? Then I’ll speak to the hospital team now about seeing you first thing tomorrow, and ask them to make sure you’re treated with respect.
model.why: Child safety, earliest alternative, addresses stigma

model.text: I’ll ask Leanne. Tomorrow morning I could do.

Good. No more ibuprofen. Don’t stop drinking suddenly — that can cause fits — and I’ll prescribe vitamin B1 and, if the hospital team agree, a stomach-protecting tablet today. I won’t start iron until you’ve been seen.

If you vomit blood, pass more black stool, feel faint, collapse or get chest pain — call 999 straight away, whatever the time. I’ll ring you back within the hour once I’ve spoken to the hospital. Can you tell me what you’ll do?
Ring Leanne now. 999 if I’m sick with blood or pass out. Wait for your call about tomorrow.

social.t: A separated father with a drinking problem may avoid services for fear of losing contact. Naming his care for Mia as a strength builds trust.
Redundancy, Universal Credit and a strained relationship with his sister limit his options; ask permission to involve her.

legal.t: Presumption of capacity; unwise decisions are allowed; capacity is decision-specific. Document the assessment.
The welfare of the child is paramount. Immediate safety (another adult present) comes first; consider safeguarding advice proportionately and transparently.

professional.t: Record the advice given, the risks explained in his words, the capacity assessment, the alternative plan, who was contacted and the safety-net.
Asking the receiving team to be aware of his previous experience is reasonable and helps engagement.

community.t: Community alcohol service (assisted withdrawal); Al-Anon and family support for his sister; Citizens Advice; Drinkline.

redFlags: Chest pain or breathlessness at rest
ice: Concern: losing contact with his daughter; being judged

playbook.diagnosis: Symptomatic microcytic anaemia from probable recurrent bleeding peptic ulcer (incomplete H. pylori eradication, NSAIDs, alcohol); high Glasgow-Blatchford score; alcohol dependence. Capacitous refusal of same-day admission.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your old stomach ulcer is very likely bleeding again, and you’ve lost about half your blood count. That can get dangerous quickly.”

management.reflectIce: “You want to protect Mia and you don’t want to be judged again. Let’s make a plan that keeps you both safer tonight and gets you seen as soon as you’re able.”
management.psychosocial: Ask Leanne to stay or take Mia; advocate for respectful care; alcohol service when stable.
sharedPlan: Recommend admission today; offer remains open
On-call medical or gastroenterology discussion today — earliest ambulatory assessment and endoscopy
PPI as agreed; stop NSAIDs; thiamine; no iron yet
Do not stop alcohol suddenly; alcohol service referral
safetyNet: 999 for vomiting blood, more black stool, faintness, collapse or chest pain
GP call-back within the hour with the hospital plan

pitfalls.intro: Candidates either accept the refusal and prescribe iron, or argue until time runs out. The station rewards finding the reason and building the safest plan he will accept.

items.fail: Explains anaemia and prescribes ferrous sulfate without asking about black stools.
items.why: Misses an active upper GI bleed with haemodynamic compromise.
items.fix: Ask about melaena, haematemesis, NSAIDs and alcohol in every unexplained anaemia.

items.fail: Accepts “no” and ends the call with “ring if worse”.
items.why: No capacity assessment, no alternative, and a child left with a parent at risk of collapse.
items.fix: Explore, explain risk, assess capacity, negotiate, protect the child, document, call back.

items.fail: Warns that social services will have to be told.
items.why: A threat confirms his fear and ends engagement; immediate safety can be secured another way.
items.fix: Frame it as Mia’s safety tonight and solve it together.

timeMap.d: Black stools, pain, NSAIDs, H. pylori, alcohol dependence.
Probable bleeding ulcer; honest risk; hospital today.
Mia and stigma; capacity; adult for Mia; on-call team; medicines.

wordPics.clearFail: Reads the results, prescribes iron, misses melaena or accepts the refusal without exploring it; no capacity assessment, no thought for the child.
wordPics.fail: Recognises the bleed and recommends admission, but argues rather than explores, does not assess capacity, or leaves no alternative plan or safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Recognises a significant upper GI bleed, recommends admission with honest risk, explores the refusal, assesses capacity, arranges another adult for Mia, contacts the on-call team and gives clear 999 advice.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, with warmth: uses his care for Mia as common ground, addresses the previous stigma, adds thiamine, NSAID and alcohol-withdrawal advice, defers iron for a reason, and closes with a call-back and teach-back.

avoid.dont: “If you won’t go, I’ll have to involve social services.”
avoid.instead: “If you collapse tonight, Mia would be alone with you — who could be with her?”
avoid.why: Solves the safety issue without a threat.

avoid.instead: “Please don’t stop suddenly — with your morning shakes that could cause fits. The alcohol team can help you cut down safely.”
avoid.why: Abrupt cessation in dependence is dangerous.

avoid.dont: “Fine, your choice — ring if it gets worse.”
avoid.instead: “It is your choice. Let’s make the safest plan around it and I’ll ring you back within the hour.”
avoid.why: Respecting autonomy still requires risk reduction and follow-up.
